en: Now, one thing we saw in the last lectures
is this glob thing here and that's another
Bun API, another native Bun API.
Glob is imported from Bun, not from Node.js.
And the idea behind glob is that you have a
mechanism for finding files and folders on
your system. So for an application like this
where I know that I want to load all my
customer JSON files here for this invoice
generation application,
I have various JSON files here for my
customers. And I'm adding more and more for
every new customer where I wanna generate an
invoice.
And therefore I don't know in advance when I
build this application how many JSON files
I'll have here, which is why I can't
hardcode those JSON file names into the
application.
That's where glob comes in. It can
dynamically find me files based on a certain
pattern we're passing to glob.
And that pattern looks like this, for
example.
Relative from the application root folder.
So from this root project folder, I have my
path here, customers, and then this asterisk
simply means I don't care about the file
name, I just care about it ending with JSON.
And there are a bunch of supported glob
patterns. The asterisk file extension one is
very common. You also will sometimes need
double asterisks if you don't care about the
folder name either or to do recursive
search. So for example, here, if I had
this pattern, I would say I don't care about
subfolders in the customers folder. So we
should dive into all those subfolders and I
wanna find all JSON files in all subfolders
inside of customers. That's how we could
write this too.
And with this change, the application would
still work, would still find those
files here, but I could now also
add a subfolder
with a JSON file in there,
company2.
And let's say in there I give it an ID of
Company 2 and Company
So I could have a subfolder in there
and now it would find that as well.
And in the invoices folder, you see the
Company 2 invoice has been generated as
well.
So that's what you can do with glob. And
there are a couple of other placeholders and
patterns as well. And I'll attach the link
to this official documentation article and
section here which lists all the supported
patterns so that you can build the pattern
or let AI build the pattern you need for
your specific use case.
And then glob just returns a glob object.
Now what is in that object?
Well, that object has a match method, a
scan, and a scan_sync method. Match is a
method where you could now pass in
a path like customers/acme.json.
And this would yield true or false depending
on whether this specific path was found with
this pattern.
So if that is in the list of identified
files and folders,
that can be useful, but more useful is scan,
which is what we're also using down here.
So I'm setting up my glob here or I'm
getting my object. And then here with scan,
we're doing the actual scanning.
And we're doing this asynchronously by
default so that we can loop through it with
an asynchronous for loop. So we have to
await here. So calling scan will then do the
actual scan and allow us to loop through the
identified files and folders step by step.
So here we then get a bunch of strings. So
we're doing the scanning on the fly and we
can process the results step by step to get
each path step by step. That's what we're
doing here. And then we're using that with
Bun file to load the specific paths. And
glob therefore is a very useful API if you
are building an application where you
need to dynamically load and process files,
but you don't know in advance what the
concrete file names will be. And therefore
you'll typically and very often use it
together with Bunfile to then process and
load the file, for example, as we're doing
it here.
